hook.line: Don Hernando watches the match and cannot remember a single name. He says who he means by what they are wearing, and never repeats the word for the players.
hook.es: Los de la camiseta roja juegan mejor.
hook.en: The ones in the red shirts play better.

examples.es: Los de la camiseta roja juegan mejor.
examples.en: The ones in the red shirts play better.

examples.es: Me gusta más la de la izquierda.
examples.en: I like the one on the left better.

examples.es:
¿Cuál es tu carro?
El de la esquina.
examples.en:
Which is your car?
The one on the corner.

examples.es: Los del café abren a las siete.
examples.en: The ones from the café open at seven.

examples.es:
¿Las llaves de la casa?
No, las del carro.
examples.en:
The house keys?
No, the car ones.

examples.es: Tres de los invitados no vinieron.
examples.en: Three of the guests didn't come.

rule:
English says "the one" or "the ones". Spanish simply drops the noun and keeps the article: *el*, *la*, *los*, *las* plus *de* plus a detail that tells you which: *los de la camiseta roja*.

The article matches the noun you left out: *la de la izquierda* (a feminine thing), *los de* (masculine plural). *De* plus *el* joins as *del*: *el del café*.

With a number: *tres de los invitados*, *dos de mis amigos*. Drop the noun only when the listener can tell what it is.
smallPrint: Teachers call this a noun left out (ellipsis): the article is doing the job of a pronoun.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *el* or *la* and type the whole sentence: *Me gusta más ___ de la izquierda.* (I like the one on the left better. You mean a house, *la casa*.)
yourTurn.answer: Me gusta más la de la izquierda.
yourTurn.why: *La* matches the missing *casa*, which is feminine.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: The ones in the red shirts play better.
yourTurn.answer: Los de la camiseta roja juegan mejor.
yourTurn.why: *Los* stands for the players, so you never repeat the noun.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I prefer the one by the window. (a masculine thing)
yourTurn.why: *El* plus *de* plus the place tells you which one.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Two of my friends live in Medellín.
yourTurn.answer: Dos de mis amigos viven en Medellín.
yourTurn.why: A number plus *de* plus the whole group says how many of them.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Vale's is sweeter. (a feminine thing)
yourTurn.answer: La de Vale es más dulce.
yourTurn.why: *La* agrees with the missing feminine noun.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about the café: *Los de la casa abren a las siete.* Say: The ones from the café open at seven.
yourTurn.answer: Los del café abren a las siete.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Five of the neighbours signed.
yourTurn.why: *De los* names the group the five come from.

pitfalls.wrong: Me gusta más la una de la izquierda.
pitfalls.right: Me gusta más la de la izquierda.
pitfalls.why: Almost. English needs "one"; Spanish needs nothing, just the article and *de*.

pitfalls.wrong: Los de el café abren a las siete.
pitfalls.right: Los del café abren a las siete.

pitfalls.why: Almost. After a number and *de*, you need the whole group: *mis*, *los*.

personal: Point out something around you without naming it: use *el de*, *la de*, *los de* or *las de* plus a detail, for example *la de la ventana*.
